The white piddock Barnea candida is a common borer in soft sedimentary rock and wood along European coasts, and its life history traits reflect a clear adaptation to a cool-temperate environment. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of this species was measured at 12% [GSI = 12%] when animals were acclimated and maintained at a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. Field surveys have further established that individuals cease somatic growth upon reaching a distinct terminal size, with the ultimate total length recorded at 3.82 cm [Li = 3.82 cm], a dimension that places Barnea candida among the medium-sized members of the Pholadidae. This asymptotic size is achieved after several years of sustained burrowing activity, during which the shell continues to enlarge until the mantle cavity reaches its maximum capacity within the confines of the excavated burrow.

Onset of reproductive capability occurs well before the animal reaches its final body dimensions, a pattern common among iteroparous molluscs that need to capitalize on early reproductive windows. The total length at puberty for Barnea candida has been determined to be 1.7 cm [Lp = 1.7 cm], meaning that individuals begin allocating resources to gametogenesis once the shell has grown to less than half of its ultimate length. This early maturation allows the species to maintain population densities even in habitats where post-settlement mortality is high, as a cohort can contribute offspring before succumbing to predation or intertidal stress. The corresponding dry weight at puberty, estimated from standard length-weight regressions, is 0.0353 g , a modest body mass that underscores the low somatic investment required to reach this developmental threshold. In contrast, the ultimate dry weight of a fully grown adult reaches 0.37 g , an increase by roughly an order of magnitude compared to the pubertal value. This tenfold increase in dry mass from puberty to senescence reflects a prolonged period of growth and tissue accumulation that supports multiple spawning events over the animal's lifetime.

The earliest life stages of Barnea candida begin with the release of fertilized eggs into the water column, where development proceeds through a brief planktonic phase. The wet weight at birth, corresponding to the mass of the newly hatched veliger larva, is remarkably low at 0.00000097 g [Wwb = 0.00000097 g], a figure derived directly from the measured egg diameter of 123 micrometres using the standard volumetric formula for a sphere. This minuscule initial mass is typical of bivalves that produce large numbers of small, planktotrophic larvae, which must feed on phytoplankton for several weeks before attaining metamorphic competence. The prodissoconch stage in these larvae is characterized by rapid cilia-driven feeding and a gradual accumulation of shell material, during which the individuals are highly vulnerable to both starvation and predation. Larvae that successfully settle and undergo metamorphosis transition into post-larval spat, initiating the boring behaviour that defines the remainder of their benthic life. The extreme fecundity necessitated by such a small birth mass ensures that a sufficient number of offspring survive the planktonic bottleneck to recruit into the adult population.

Longevity studies conducted under controlled laboratory conditions have provided a clear estimate of the species' maximum lifespan. Barnea candida maintained in recirculating seawater aquaria at a constant temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] have been recorded to survive for a maximum of 1825 days [am = 1825 days], a duration equivalent to approximately five years. This lifespan is relatively extended for a pholad bivalve of its size, a pattern that may be linked to the protective nature of its burrowing habitat, which reduces predation risk and physical disturbance from wave action. The slow, steady growth observed in these individuals culminates in the attainment of a terminal adult shell size of 3.82 cm [Li = 3.82 cm] after several years, a pattern consistent with a life history that prioritizes longevity over rapid maturation. Field observations support these laboratory findings, with the largest individuals collected from intertidal chalk exposures generally falling within the size range predicted by a five-year maximum lifespan.

The reproductive ecology of Barnea candida is tightly coupled to seasonal temperature cycles, with spawning events typically concentrated during the warmer months when food availability for planktonic larvae is highest. Populations inhabiting regions with a stable water temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C] exhibit a well-defined pattern of reproductive maturation and output. At this thermal regime, the attainment of a shell length of 1.7 cm [Lp = 1.7 cm] signals the transition to reproductive capability, with a corresponding dry tissue mass of approximately 0.0353 g  at that threshold. The maximum dry body mass of an adult individual reaches 0.37 g , after which virtually all resources are invested in gamete production until senescence. The gonadosomatic index was 12% [GSI = 12%] at a temperature of 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The remarkably low wet weight at birth of 0.00000097 g [Wwb = 0.00000097 g] completes the life history picture, highlighting the trade-off between offspring size and number that underpins the species' reproductive strategy.
